new_quiz.q: What is color grading?
choices: Changing the colors and contrast of the final image
Painting colors on the vertices of a mesh
Choosing the Base Color of a material
Sorting textures by their color
new_quiz.explain: Color grading works on the finished picture, like editing a photo. It changes the mood without touching the scene itself.

new_quiz.q: Where do you grade a scene in Unreal Engine?
choices: In the Material Editor
In the World Settings
In a Post Process Volume
In the Content Browser
new_quiz.explain: The Post Process Volume holds the Color Grading settings. With Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on, the grade applies to the whole level.

new_quiz.q: What is a LUT?
choices: A light that only affects reflections
A lookup table: a small texture that stores a color grade
A list of the lights in the level
A tool that measures the exposure
new_quiz.explain: LUT means lookup table. It stores a color grade made in an image editor, so that the same grade can be applied in the engine.

new_quiz.q: What can color grading not do?
choices: Change the contrast of the image
Make the image warmer or cooler
Darken the shadows
Fix bad lighting
new_quiz.explain: Grading finishes an image. If the lighting is wrong, the grade only changes the colors of a badly lit picture, so you grade last, after lighting.

new_quiz.q: In which order do you grade by hand in this quest?
choices: Highlights first, then the white balance, then the global settings
Shadows first, then the LUT, then the white balance
The white balance first, then the global settings, then shadows, midtones and highlights
The global settings first, then the LUT, then the midtones
new_quiz.explain: You go from the broad to the fine. White balance sets the base, the global settings shape the whole image, and the three ranges are adjusted last.

new_quiz.q: What is the neutral LUT image that you download from the Epic documentation?
choices: A LUT that changes nothing yet
A LUT that turns the image gray
A screenshot of an empty level
A texture with a single color
new_quiz.explain: The neutral LUT is the starting point, 256 x 16 pixels in size. It only becomes a grade after you apply your adjustments to it.

new_quiz.q: Why do you apply the same color adjustments to the screenshot and to the LUT image in the image editor?
choices: So both files get the same size
So the screenshot can be imported as a LUT
So the LUT image is deleted afterwards
The screenshot shows the result, and the LUT image records the adjustments
new_quiz.explain: You judge the grade on the screenshot. The same adjustments on the LUT image store that grade in a form Unreal can apply.

new_quiz.q: Which settings do you change on the imported LUT texture?
choices: Texture Group to World and Mip Gen Settings to Sharpen0
Texture Group to ColorLookupTable and Mip Gen Settings to NoMipmaps
Texture Group to UI and sRGB turned off
Texture Group to Lightmap and Mip Gen Settings to Blur1
new_quiz.explain: A LUT is data and not a normal picture. These two settings keep Unreal from shrinking or filtering it in a way that would change the colors.

new_quiz.q: Where do you assign the LUT texture?
choices: In the Light Color of the Directional Light
In the Emissive Color of a material
In the Post Process Volume, as the Color Grading LUT
In the World Settings, under Lightmass
new_quiz.explain: The Color Grading LUT slot is in the Misc part of the Color Grading settings of the Post Process Volume.

new_quiz.q: Why do you keep one screenshot without any grade?
choices: As a reference to compare the graded stills with
Because the LUT needs it during play
Because Unreal deletes ungraded levels
As the icon of the level
new_quiz.explain: After some time with a grade, the eye gets used to it. The ungraded still shows what the grade really changed.

new_quiz.q: What is Movie Render Queue?
choices: The list of levels that are loaded at start
The tool in Unreal for rendering final images and videos
A panel that plays videos inside the editor
A plugin that records the screen during play
new_quiz.explain: Movie Render Queue, often shortened to MRQ, renders final frames. It is what you use when a normal screenshot is not clean enough.

new_quiz.q: Why is a Movie Render Queue image cleaner than a normal screenshot?
choices: It uses a different level
It removes the lights before rendering
It always renders in black and white
It can spend more time on each frame than the viewport does
new_quiz.explain: The viewport must draw many frames each second. Movie Render Queue has no such limit, so it can render one frame with much more care.

new_quiz.q: What does Movie Render Queue render from?
choices: A Level Sequence
A camera bookmark
A Widget Blueprint
A Material Instance
new_quiz.explain: A Level Sequence is the asset Unreal uses for cinematics. Movie Render Queue renders its frames.

new_quiz.q: How long is the Level Sequence you create for a still image?
choices: One second
Ten frames
One frame
One minute
new_quiz.explain: A still is a single picture, so the sequence only needs one frame.

new_quiz.q: Why must the Level Sequence have a Camera Cut track?
choices: So the sequence loops
So the render uses your Cine Camera
So the camera moves during the frame
So the frame is saved as a video
new_quiz.explain: The Camera Cut track tells the sequence which camera to look through. Without it, the render does not use the view you framed.

new_quiz.q: What do anti-aliasing samples do in Movie Render Queue?
choices: They add more lights to the scene
They make the image file smaller
They raise the frame rate of the viewport
They smooth jagged edges by rendering the frame several times
new_quiz.explain: Each sample is one more render of the same frame. Combined, they give smooth edges and less noise.

new_quiz.q: Why do you save the render settings as a preset?
choices: So you can use them again later
So the render runs in the background
So the Level Sequence gets longer
So the camera is locked
new_quiz.explain: A preset stores your settings. The next render starts from it, and all your stills get the same quality.

new_quiz.q: What do you compare the Movie Render Queue still with?
choices: A photo of your monitor
A render of a different level
A High Resolution Screenshot of the same frame
A still from another camera
new_quiz.explain: The same frame taken both ways shows exactly what Movie Render Queue adds. Look at the edges and at fine detail.

new_quiz.q: The rendered still shows a different view from the one you framed. What do you check first?
choices: That the level has a Sky Light
That the Level Sequence has a Camera Cut track with your Cine Camera
That the preset has a name
That the resolution is high
new_quiz.explain: The render looks through the camera of the Camera Cut track. If the track is missing or uses another camera, you get another view.

new_quiz.q: Which two choices in the render settings raise the quality of the still in this quest?
choices: A lower frame rate and a shorter sequence
A second Level Sequence and a second camera
A smaller file type and fewer lights
Anti-aliasing samples and a high resolution
new_quiz.explain: The samples smooth the edges and the high resolution keeps fine detail. Together they are the main reasons the still beats a screenshot.

new_quiz.q: What is a reference scene?
choices: A neutral level with known lighting that people use to check their assets
The first level of a finished game
A folder with reference images
A level that shows every material of a project
new_quiz.explain: A reference scene is a known, neutral place. People put an asset into it to see how the asset looks under fixed conditions.

new_quiz.q: Why should everyone on a team check assets in the same reference scene?
choices: The scene makes all assets look the same
The scene fixes mistakes in the assets
Everyone judges under the same light, so the results can be compared
Only one person can then open the assets
new_quiz.explain: An asset looks different under every light. With one shared scene, a difference between two assets comes from the assets and not from the lighting.

new_quiz.q: What is a Macbeth-style swatch board?
choices: A board that lists the names of the cameras
A board of standard color patches
A board with the README text
A board that blocks the key light
new_quiz.explain: The patches have known colors. If they look wrong in the picture, the lighting or the exposure is off.

new_quiz.q: Which pair of balls belongs in the scene?
choices: One red and one blue
One large and one small
One lit and one unlit
One gray and one chrome
new_quiz.explain: The gray ball shows how the light falls on a plain surface. The chrome ball mirrors the surroundings, so you see where the light comes from.

new_quiz.q: How do you give the reference scene a fixed exposure?
choices: Add a Post Process Volume and set Metering Mode to Manual
Set the Directional Light to Movable
Turn off Lumen in the Project Settings
Save a camera bookmark at each camera
new_quiz.explain: With Manual metering the camera does not adjust the brightness by itself. Every asset is then judged at the same exposure.

new_quiz.q: What is the hero area of the reference scene?
choices: The place where the cameras stand
The place where the README is shown
The place where the asset stands
The place with the swatch board
new_quiz.explain: The hero area is where people put their asset. The three lights show its shape from the front, in the shadows and along its edge.

new_quiz.q: How are the surfaces of the scene built?
choices: From a new material for every surface
From one master material with instances
From vertex colors only
From decals on a single mesh
new_quiz.explain: One master material with instances keeps the scene easy to maintain. It also uses at least one Material Function, and one prop has a vertex-painted blend.

new_quiz.q: What do you provide so that people can take the same pictures of every asset?
choices: A list of console commands
A second copy of the level
A folder of screenshots
3 Cine Cameras with bookmarks, and a Movie Render Queue preset
new_quiz.explain: Fixed cameras give the same views each time. The preset gives the same render settings, so stills of different assets can be compared.

new_quiz.q: What must the one-page README say?
choices: How to use the scene, what the exposure is, and what people should not change
How long the scene took to build and which tools you used
Which assets were tested in the scene so far
Which engine versions you tried
new_quiz.explain: The README is the manual for other people. It protects the fixed parts of the scene, such as the exposure, from changes by mistake.

new_quiz.q: What does the mentor check about your README?
choices: That it is longer than one page
That it lists every node of the master material
That the scene could be used with only your README
That it is written before the scene is built
new_quiz.explain: The scene is built for other people. If someone can use it with nothing but the README, the guide does its job.

new_quiz.q: What is set dressing?
choices: Choosing clothes for a character
Filling a scene with small objects such as rocks and debris
Setting the lights of a scene
Naming the assets of a project
new_quiz.explain: Set dressing adds the many small objects that make a place look real. Placing each one by hand takes a long time.

new_quiz.q: How does PCG help with set dressing?
choices: It lowers the triangle count of each rock
It paints textures on the landscape
It imports rock meshes from Fab
You build a graph of rules, and the graph places many objects for you
new_quiz.explain: PCG means Procedural Content Generation. The rules place the objects, so you change a rule and not a thousand rocks.

new_quiz.q: PCG is missing from the right-click menu of the Content Browser. What do you check first?
choices: That the Procedural Content Generation Framework (PCG) plugin is enabled
That the level has a Landscape
That the project has a rock mesh
That the Place Actors panel is open
new_quiz.explain: PCG comes from a plugin. You enable it in Edit, then Plugins, and the PCG entries appear in the editor.

new_quiz.q: In which order do you connect the three nodes of the scatter graph?
choices: Surface Sampler, Static Mesh Spawner, Get Landscape Data
Static Mesh Spawner, Get Landscape Data, Surface Sampler
Get Landscape Data, Surface Sampler, Static Mesh Spawner
Surface Sampler, Get Landscape Data, Static Mesh Spawner
new_quiz.explain: The graph first reads the landscape, then makes points on its surface, and last puts a mesh on each point.

new_quiz.q: What does the Surface Sampler node do in this graph?
choices: It reads the height of the camera
It makes points on the surface of the landscape
It picks the mesh that is spawned
It deletes the landscape under the rocks
new_quiz.explain: The sampler turns the landscape surface into many points. Each point can later become one object.

new_quiz.q: How do you run the graph in the level?
choices: Drag the graph asset onto the landscape
Press Play and wait
Open the graph and press F9
Place a PCG Volume, set Graph on its PCG component, and click Generate
new_quiz.explain: The PCG Volume marks where the graph works. Its PCG component needs to know the graph, and Generate runs it.

new_quiz.q: What does a density rule control?
choices: How many objects appear
How heavy each object is
How bright each object is
How large the PCG Volume is
new_quiz.explain: A density rule thins out or keeps points. A Density Filter node after the Surface Sampler is one way to build it.

new_quiz.q: What does an exclusion rule do?
choices: It adds objects to an area
It changes the mesh of the objects
It removes objects from an area
It hides the PCG Volume
new_quiz.explain: An exclusion rule takes points away where you do not want objects. That is how a path stays free.

new_quiz.q: Which node can subtract the points near a spline along the path?
choices: A Static Mesh Spawner node
A Difference node
A Get Landscape Data node
A Surface Sampler node
new_quiz.explain: A Difference node removes one set of points from another. With the points near the path spline as the second set, the path is kept clear.

new_quiz.q: Why do you add a rule that keeps the paths clear?
choices: So the graph has more nodes
So the rocks are larger near the path
So the PCG Volume can be deleted
So the scattered objects do not block where the player walks
new_quiz.explain: A scatter that covers everything also covers the route. The rule keeps the dressing where it helps the scene and away from the path.

new_quiz.q: What is the Water system in Unreal Engine?
choices: A material that makes any mesh look wet
A weather tool that makes rain
A plugin that gives you ready-made lakes, rivers and oceans
A view mode that shows reflections
new_quiz.explain: The Water system comes as the Water plugin. It adds water bodies that you place in a level.

new_quiz.q: Why does water have a strong effect on the mood of a scene?
choices: It reflects everything around it
It makes the level load more slowly
It turns off the other lights
It hides the landscape under it
new_quiz.explain: Water mirrors the sky and the surroundings. Clear, bright water and dark, murky water give the same place two very different moods.

new_quiz.q: What do you do right after you enable the Water plugin in Edit, then Plugins?
choices: Delete the Landscape
Restart the editor
Create a new project
Open the Material Editor
new_quiz.explain: A plugin only loads when the editor starts. After the restart, the water bodies are available.

new_quiz.q: How do you add a lake or a river to the level?
choices: Sculpt a hole and fill it with a blue material
Right-click in the Content Browser and choose Water
Open Landscape Mode and choose New
Search for Water Body in the Place Actors panel and drag one into the level
new_quiz.explain: The Place Actors panel lists Water Body Lake and Water Body River after the plugin is enabled. You drag one into the level.

new_quiz.q: Where do you find the material of a water body?
choices: In Water Material in the Details panel of the water body
In the World Settings of the level
In the Landscape Material of the Landscape
In the Post Process Volume
new_quiz.explain: You select the water body and look for Water Material in its Details panel. It points to a Material Instance.

new_quiz.q: Why do you make a copy of the water Material Instance before you change it?
choices: A copy renders faster than the original
The original cannot be opened
So the original of the plugin stays as it is
So the water body gets collision
new_quiz.explain: The original instance belongs to the plugin and can be used by other water bodies. Changing a copy keeps your tuning in your own asset.

new_quiz.q: Which two values of the copied Material Instance do you change to tune the water?
choices: Roughness and Metallic
Absorption and Scattering
Intensity and Source Angle
Inner Radius and Falloff Distance
new_quiz.explain: Absorption and Scattering describe what happens to light inside the water. Together they set its color and how far you can see into it.

new_quiz.q: What does Scattering control?
choices: How fast the water flows
How high the waves are
How large the lake is
How light spreads inside the water
new_quiz.explain: Scattering is how light spreads inside the water. It changes how clear or murky the water looks.

new_quiz.q: Why do you write one line about the mood before you tune the water?
choices: It gives you a target to tune toward and to judge the result against
The plugin reads the line and sets the values
The line is used as the name of the water body
It replaces the screenshot as proof
new_quiz.explain: Clear and tropical needs different values from dark and murky. With the mood written down, you know when the water is right.

new_quiz.q: The water values look right, but the water still feels wrong for the mood. What else should you look at?
choices: The name of the level
The size of the Content Browser
The sky and the lighting around the water
The number of camera bookmarks
new_quiz.explain: Water reflects everything around it. If the sky does not fit the mood, the water will not fit it either.

new_quiz.q: What is a Procedural Foliage Volume?
choices: A brush that paints single plants by hand
A box that fills an area with plants by simulating how they spread
A volume that hides plants from the camera
A folder that stores tree meshes
new_quiz.explain: The volume simulates how plants spread and places them inside its box. You do not place each tree yourself.

new_quiz.q: What do foliage types act like in this system?
choices: Like materials on a mesh
Like lights in a room
Like cameras in a shot
Like species with their own spacing rules
new_quiz.explain: Each foliage type is one kind of plant. Its settings say how it spreads and how much room it needs.

new_quiz.q: Why do the spacing settings matter so much?
choices: Plants with the same distance between them look artificial
Plants that are too close cannot be saved
Plants only cast shadows at one distance
Plants need spacing to get collision
new_quiz.explain: Real forests are uneven. Even spacing looks like a plantation, so you tune the rules until the result is not uniform.

new_quiz.q: The Procedural Foliage Spawner is missing from the Foliage menu of the Content Browser. What do you check first?
choices: That the Water plugin is enabled
That the level is saved
That Procedural Foliage is enabled in the Editor Preferences
That Nanite is enabled on the tree meshes
new_quiz.explain: Procedural Foliage is an experimental feature. You turn it on in Edit, then Editor Preferences, in the Experimental section.

new_quiz.q: Which assets do you create for a volume with 2 species?
choices: Two Landscape Grass Type assets and one PCG Graph
Two Static Mesh Foliage assets and one Procedural Foliage Spawner
Two Material Instances and one master material
Two Level Instances and one Data Asset
new_quiz.explain: Each species is one Static Mesh Foliage asset with its own mesh and rules. The spawner holds the list of species.

new_quiz.q: Where do you add the two species in the spawner?
choices: Under Mesh Entries
Under Grass Types
Under Parameter Name
Under Foliage Types
new_quiz.explain: The spawner has a list named Foliage Types. Every Static Mesh Foliage asset in that list takes part in the simulation.

new_quiz.q: How do you make the spawner fill the forest edge?
choices: Drag it into the level, scale it over the area, and click Resimulate
Open it and click Generate
Paint it on the landscape in Foliage Mode
Add it to the Landscape Material
new_quiz.explain: The spawner in the level becomes the volume. Resimulate in its Details panel runs the simulation inside the scaled box.

new_quiz.q: Which of these are spacing settings of a Static Mesh Foliage asset?
choices: Inner Radius, Falloff Distance and Apply Reverb
Source Angle, Intensity and Light Color
Shade Radius, Initial Seed Density and Average Spread Distance
Absorption, Scattering and Roughness
new_quiz.explain: These settings control how many plants start, how far they spread, and how much room each one takes. You tune them in both species.

new_quiz.q: You changed Average Spread Distance, but the forest in the level looks the same. What do you do?
choices: Restart the editor
Click Resimulate in the Details panel of the volume
Delete the Landscape
Enable Procedural Foliage again
new_quiz.explain: The plants in the level are the result of the last simulation. A changed setting only shows after you click Resimulate.

new_quiz.q: When is the tuning of the forest edge finished?
choices: When both species have the same settings
When every tree has the same distance to the next
When the volume holds no plants
When the edge of the forest looks natural and not uniform
new_quiz.explain: The goal is a result that looks grown and not placed. You keep tuning both species together until the edge reads as natural.
